segments.text: Big idea! The entire book of Daniel culminates not in an empire or an earthly kingdom,
but in a living, divine person. Michael, Jesus Christ, stands up for his people.
A time of trouble follows, everyone written in the book is delivered,
and the sleeping saints wake from the dust in literal bodily resurrection to everlasting life.
Daniel 12, 1-2. In plain words, Daniel 10-12 is one unbroken prophecy.
Christ, as Michael, stands up. A time of trouble follows. Those written in the book are saved.
The dead rise. From the last sitting, sitting 9.
In sitting 9, Gabriel returned to answer Daniel's prayer and solve the unexplained
2,300 days of Daniel 8. Sitting 9 counted 70 weeks, 490 years, from Artaxerxes' decree in 457 B.C.,
the year the command went out to restore and to build Jerusalem. Ezra 7, Daniel 9.25.
Those weeks landed on the baptism of Messiah in A.D. 27 and on his crucifixion in the middle
of the 70th week, A.D. 31. Daniel counted the 70 weeks as years because the visions of Daniel
measure time the same way they measure beasts and horns. One prophetic day stands for one year of
real history. Numbers 1434, Ezekiel 4-6, the scale sitting zero laid out. Daniel 9 then tested
that scale and it fit. 483 years to the baptism, the cross in the middle of the last seven.
Because the same scale holds, the 2,300 days of Daniel 8 are 2,300 years and they run from the
same 457 B.C. start to 1844, Daniel 8.14. Now, in the third year of Cyrus, 536-535 B.C.,
Daniel receives the final panoramic revelation of the book, an unbroken prophetic narrative
stretching from the Persian court to the resurrection of the dead. Introduction,
the final vision by the great river Hidical, Tigris. Daniel 10.1-4, Hidical. The Tigris, 536-535 B.C.
In the third year of Cyrus, King of Persia, 536-535 B.C., a revelation was given to Daniel,
whose name was called Belteshazzar, Daniel 10.1. The decree of Cyrus had already permitted the
exiles to return to Jerusalem, Ezra 1-4, yet only a small remnant had returned and there was fierce
local opposition to the rebuilding of the temple, Ezra 4-5. Deeply burdened for the future of his
people and the holy city, the aged prophet entered a three-week partial fast, eating no pleasant
bread, meat, or wine, nor anointing himself at all for three full weeks. Daniel 10.2-3.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Nisan, Esther 3.7, as Daniel stood beside the
great river Hidical, the ancient name for the Tigris, he lifted up his eyes and looked upon
an awe-inspiring celestial vision. Structural Unity. Chapters 10.11-12. Form 1. Single Vision.
1. Section. Daniel 10.1-12.4. In 536-535 B.C. Daniel 12.5-13 continues at the river after 12.4.
Chapter 10 is the prologue and theophany. Daniel fasts by the Tigris. The glorious man in
linen appears. Gabriel pulls back the veil on the unseen cosmic warfare behind earthly empires.
Chapter 11 is the detailed march of history. Gabriel narrates literal geopolitical history
in advance without symbolic beasts, from Persian succession, through Alexander the Great and the
Hellenistic Ptolemaic-slash-Solucid wars, to pagan Rome, the crucifixion of the Prince of
the Covenant, 1122, and the blasphemous career of Papal Rome, 1131-39. Chapter 12 is the end
of the story. Michael stands up. A time of trouble such as never was breaks upon the earth.
The saints written in the book are delivered, the dead are raised from the dust, and Daniel
is given God's personal promise. Main Point 1. The Theophany. The man clothed in linen
and cosmic warfare. Daniel 10.5-14.20-21. Revelation 1.13-15. As Daniel stood by the
Tigris, he was granted a direct Christophany, a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ.
Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold, a certain man clothed in linen,
whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz. His body also was like the barrel,
and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his
feet like in color to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
Daniel 10.5-6.KJV. This inventory overlaps the glorified Christ revealed to John on Patmos,
Revelation 1.13-15. Linen and gold, eyes as fire, metal brightness.
It is not a word-for-word match. Daniel 10.6 has a voice like a multitude. Revelation 1.15
has many waters. John's white hair is not in Daniel 10. The overlap still reads priestly,
royal, and military Christ. Unseen spiritual warfare, the princes behind earthly monarchies.
Daniel was overcome by the divine glory and fell to the ground in deep sleep. An angel, Gabriel,
touched him, set him on his knees, and revealed why his answer had taken three weeks to arrive.
Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand,
and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days, but lo,
Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
Daniel 10.12-13.KJV. This remarkable passage pulls back the curtain of the invisible world.
The prince of the kingdom of Persia was not an earthly king,
but Satan's demonic agent working upon the Persian court to influence Cyrus against the
Jewish exiles. Ephesians 6.12. For twenty-one days, the exact duration of Daniel's fast,
Gabriel wrestled against these dark demonic powers. Finally, Michael, the supreme prince of heaven,
arrived on the battlefield, broke the satanic resistance, and secured favor for God's covenant
people. Who is Michael? In Hebrew, the name Mikael asks, who is like God? He is the prince
who stands for Daniel's people, Daniel 12.1, and the one who comes to help the angel speaking in
Daniel 10.13. Jude 9 names Michael the archangel, and Revelation 12.7 names him as the commander
who casts out the dragon. Here is why this reading takes Michael to be Jesus in his kingly
office. 1 Thessalonians 4.16 says the Lord comes down with the voice of the archangel,
and Jesus himself says the dead shall hear his voice. John 5.28. The voice that wakes the dead
is called the voice of the archangel, and it is also the voice of the Son. This reading
holds that one person stands behind both names. Main point 2. The prophetic panorama of Daniel
11. From Persia to the end of time. Daniel 11.2-45. In Daniel 11, Gabriel unfolds the longest,
most detailed literal historical prophecy in the Bible. Unlike the symbolic animals of chapters
7 and 8, chapter 11 narrates geopolitical events in direct historical sequence. One phrase needs
its meaning fixed before the list, because the list uses it more than once. The time of the
end is the long closing stretch of history, the last part of the road, not one single day,
and not the last day itself. This reading marks one event inside that stretch, 1798, when papal
power was wounded. The trouble, the standing up of Michael, and the waking of the dead come later,
at the very end of the stretch. The unbroken historical chain of Daniel 11.1. The Persian
will stand up yet three kings in Persia, and the fourth shall be far richer than they all,
and by his strength, through his riches, he shall stir up all against the realm of Grisha.
Following Cyrus, three kings arose. Cambyses, 530-522 BC, the false Smirdas,
522 BC, and Darius I, 522-486 BC. The immensely wealthy fourth king was Xerxes I,
the Ahazuerus of Esther, 486-465 BC, who stirred up Persia against Greece in 480 BC too.
Alexander the Great and the Diadochi, 11-3-4. And a mighty king shall stand up,
and when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided toward the
four winds of heaven, and not to his posterity. Alexander conquered the Persian empire. He died
at the age of 32. His empire was divided among his four generals. The four were Cassander,
Lysimachus, Seleucus, and Ptolemy. The verse says not to his posterity. Daniel 11.4.
3. Hellenistic Wars, Kings of the North and South, 11.5-15.
Syria slash Mesopotamia under the Seleucids became the King of the North, geographically
north of Judea, while Egypt under the Ptolemies became the King of the South,
south of Judea. Their dynastic conflicts, treaties, and battles raged back and forth
across the land of Israel. 4. Imperial Pagan Rome, 11.16-22.
In verse 16, a new power comes against the King of the North. None shall stand before him,
and he stands in the glorious land, which is Judea. This reading names that power Rome,
which entered the Levant under Pompey, 63 BC, and Julius Caesar. Under Tiberius Caesar,
the Prince of the Covenant was broken. Daniel 11.22. This reading takes that to be the crucifixion of
Jesus Christ on Calvary, Luke 23.33, in A.D. 31 under Roman civil authority, Pontius Pilate,
Matthew 27.2. The reason is an echo from Daniel 9. There, the Messiah is called the Prince,
9.25, and the angel speaks of confirming the Covenant, 9.27. The Prince of the Covenant
joins both words. Some critical scholars read the Prince of the Covenant as Onias III,
the high priest in Jerusalem in the second century BC, because they date the chapter
to the troubles of that century. This course follows the echo of Daniel 9.
5. Papal Rome Phase, 11.31-39. Roman power transitions into the ecclesiastical phase.
Arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength,
and shall take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate.
11.31. The Hebrew behind daily is again Tamed. Just as in Daniel 7.25 and Daniel 8.11-12,
this power usurps Christ's heavenly priesthood, persecutes the faithful saints for a time,
times, and half a time, and exalts itself above all gods.
6. The Time of the End 11.40-45. And at the time of the end shall the king of the south push
at him. 11.40. This reading marks the time of the end at 1798, when General Berthier captured
Pope Pius VI. That capture closes the period of 1,260 years this course has already counted.
The Time and Times and the Dividing of Time, of Daniel 7.25, read on the year-day scale as
1,260 years of rule, sitting 7. The number that lands on 1798 here is 1,290, and it is written
in Daniel 12.11, not in Chapter 11. The 1,290 is counted from a start year this sitting reconstructs
as 508 by the arithmetic shown in the chart below. The rise of papal power was gradual.
The same is true of its decline. Though the papacy continued, its power was shorn, so 1798
marks the end of the prophetic period rather than a single day on which papal power vanished.
Verses 40-45 outline the final geopolitical conflicts leading up to the close of human
history. Where the Chain Ends The angel does not stop in the second century before Christ.
He carries the story to the Time of the End, 1140, then to the King who plants his tents
between the seas in the glorious holy mountain, and comes to his end with none to help him,
1145. A King who reaches his end at the close of history is not Antiochus,
who died in 164 BC. Chapter 12 then follows at once. Michael stands up, trouble comes,
the book delivers, the dead awake. Why this chapter does not stop at Antiochus?
Some readers say the King in Daniel 1121-35 is Antiochus the fourth epiphanies of the second
century BC and that the chapter's story ends with him. This is the Preterist reading.
The chapter gives three reasons to read further. It says how far it reaches. The angel comes to
explain what shall befall thy people in the latter days, Daniel 1014. A story that ends in 164 BC
does not reach the latter days. It points to Daniel 9. Verse 22 says, the Prince of the
Covenant is broken. That joins two words from Daniel 9, Prince, 925, and Covenant, 927,
where the Messiah is cut off after the 69 weeks. This reading dates that to AD 31,
long after Antiochus. It ends with the end. Verse 40 says, at the time of the end,
the long closing stretch of history. This reading starts that stretch at 1798 when papal power was
wounded, then reads verses 40-45 as the conflicts of the final years that follow 1798. The King
of the South is not named in the verse, and this reading does not name him. Then chapter 12
closes with Michael standing up, the dead awaking, and Daniel's rest at the end of the days,
Daniel 12, 1-2, 13. The death of Antiochus in 164 BC is not the end of anything.
In plain words, Daniel 11 is one long road that runs to the end of the world. The Preterist
reading gets off it at Antiochus. This course stays on it to the end. We have come to the
first checkpoint. Main point three, Michael stands up, the royal stance and the time of
trouble. Daniel 12, 1-11, 2-4, Hebrews 7, 25. The entire prophetic narrative of Daniel 10-11
reaches its supreme climax in the opening words of chapter 12. And at that time shall Michael
stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people, and there shall be a
time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time. And at that time,
thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.
Daniel 12, 1, KJV. The meaning of stand up, amad, in Daniel's prophetic grammar.
In Daniel's inspired vocabulary, the Hebrew verb amad, to stand up, consistently designates a king
assuming sovereign executive reign or entering royal authority. Daniel 11-2. There shall stand up,
amad, yet three kings in Persia. Daniel 11-3. A mighty king shall stand up, amad. Daniel 11-4.
When he shall stand up, amad, his kingdom shall be broken. Daniel 11-7, 20-21. Kings
stand up in their estates to rule. The same verb then carries over to the one the angel calls
the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people, Daniel 12-1, and the word before it
fixes its sense. A prince is a ruler. So when Daniel 12-1 declares that Michael shall stand up,
it signifies that Jesus Christ is taking up his royal rule. The verb is the same in both places,
and the subject in Daniel 12-1 is a prince, so the standing there is a king taking power.
When Michael stands up, the time of turning ends. Two words carry that sentence, so here they are
in plain words. Probation is the time of testing, the years in which a person can still turn to God
and change. Intercession is Jesus pleading the value of his own sacrifice for sinners before
the Father. The ministry Hebrews 7.25 describes when it says he ever liveth to make intercession.
Here is why that pleading ends when Michael stands. Intercession asks for people while
they can still turn. When the turning ends, there is nothing left to ask for,
and the king stands to settle what each life has chosen.
In Daniel's grammar, stand up is a king taking power. 11, 2 to 4, 7, 20 to 21. Michael is the
great prince which standeth for the children of thy people. He stands as king for those written
in the book. Hebrews 7.25 is the ministry of this age. He ever liveth to make intercession.
Daniel 12.1 is the moment that priestly work is finished and the king stands.
Then the settled word of Revelation 22.11. He that is unjust, let him be unjust still.
And he which is filthy, let him be filthy still. And he that is righteous,
let him be righteous still. And he that is holy, let him be holy still.
Revelation 22.11, KJV. We have come to the second checkpoint.
Main point 4. The great time of trouble and deliverance in the book of life.
Daniel 12.1, Jeremiah 37, Revelation 3.5, 2012-15. Daniel 12.1 itself says,
A trouble such as never was, at the time Michael stands and, on this reading,
his intercession is finished. This reading pictures that trouble in two ways,
as the Holy Spirit withdrawn from the impenitent and as the seven last plagues of Revelation 16.
Impenitent means unrepentant, people who will not turn from their sin. The seven last plagues are
the final judgments God pours out on a world that has refused his mercy, the last seven bowls
of Revelation 16. Here is the reason this reading gives for the withdrawal. The Spirit is
the one who calls people to turn. When that call has been refused to the end, the Spirit
stops striving and gives the stubborn what they have chosen, and the plagues are the removal of
the last restraint. Everyone written in the book is still delivered. Jeremiah described this same
climactic ordeal as the time of Jacob's trouble, Jeremiah 37. And at that time thy people shall
be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book. Daniel 12.1, KJV.
What does Revelation 22.11 add to that? It shows the other side of the same hour. Once the time
of turning ends, people stay as they are. To be unjust, filthy, righteous, or holy still is to
be fixed in that state. That is why the standing of Michael is spoken of as the close of probation
and not as another chance. Deliverance in the heavenly registry, the book of life.
Notice the only qualifying criterion for divine deliverance. Not political connections, material
wealth, or denominational pride, but having your name written in the book. Throughout scripture,
this celestial register is called the book of life, Philippians 4.3, Revelation 3.5,
2012-15, 21-27. Those who have surrendered their hearts to Jesus Christ, whose sins have been
washed in the blood of the Lamb, and whose names remain inscribed in the registry of heaven,
will experience ultimate divine deliverance and resurrection. Daniel 12.1-2.
Here is why being written in the book goes with surrender. The book is God's register of those
who belong to Him, and Jesus Himself told His disciples to rejoice that their names are written
in heaven, Luke 10.20. Turning from sin to Christ is how a name comes to be written there,
and holding fast to Him is how it stays. Main point 5. Bodily resurrection.
Waking from the dust and the 1,290-1,335 days. Daniel 12.2-4.11-13. John 5.28-29.
1 Thessalonians 4.16-17. Daniel 12.2 delivers the Old Testament's most explicit and glorious
declaration of literal bodily resurrection. And many of them that sleep in the dust of the
dust shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
Daniel 12.2. KJV. A literal, physical bodily awakening, not a metaphor. Some critical scholars
read Daniel 12.2 as a poetic picture of the Jewish nation rising again as a nation,
not of dead bodies coming out of the ground. In plain words, they take the verse as a picture
of the nation coming back to life after a crushing defeat. They hold this because the
book was written, they say, in a time of national crisis and revival. This reading does not accept
that. Sleeping in the Dust. In Genesis 3.19, humanity was formed from dust and returns
to dust at death. Throughout scripture, death is an unconscious sleep. Psalm 146.4, Ecclesiastes 9.5,
John 11.11-14. The dead do not hover as disembodied ghosts, they sleep in the grave
awaiting the resurrection morning. Confirmed by Jesus Christ.
John 5.28-29 stands as a parallel to Daniel 12.2. Marvel not at this, for the hour is coming,
in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth, they that have
done good, unto the resurrection of life, and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection
of damnation. Many, not a metaphor. Daniel 12.2 speaks of many who sleep in the dust,
awaking to two destinies. That is the Old Testament's clear promise of bodily resurrection.
Revelation 1.7 and Matthew 26.64 add that those who pierced him will see his appearing.
Do not flatten 12.2 into a political metaphor, and do not treat later readings of many
as if they were stated in the biblical text. The numbered spans of Daniel 12.
The 1,290 and 1,335 days. In Daniel 12.11-12, two final prophetic spans are revealed from the
time the tamede is taken away and the abomination of desolation is set up. And from the time that
the daily sacrifice shall be taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up,
there shall be 1,290 days. Blessed is he that waiteth, and cometh to the 1,305 and 30 days.
Daniel 12.11-12, KJV. This sitting applies the year-day principle to these periods,
Numbers 14.34, Ezekiel 4.6, reading the 1,290 and 1,335 days as solar years.
The verses measure from one pair of events, the taking away of the daily and the setting up of
the abomination that makes desolate, Daniel 12.11. Here is how this sitting gets a year out of that.
On this reading, the daily is Christ's continual priesthood, which sitting eight set out,
and the power that took it away is the Roman church acting with the arm of the state.
That arrangement took shape in the West when a Frankish king put his power behind the Roman
church, so this timeline starts the count when that support was in place.
AD 508, a chosen marker and not a year Daniel prints.
The arithmetic shows why it has to be 508 and not 496 or 507. Only 508 plus 1,290
lands on 1798, the year the popes lost their civil rule, and 508 plus 1,335 lands on 1843,
the year of waiting before 1844. Clovis's baptism is often dated 496, which is the king's own
adoption of the faith, and the battle of Vouillée is 507, a battlefield victory.
Both belong to the same story and both move the same cause forward,
but this count does not start from either one. It starts when that backing was in place,
and the two events of Daniel 1211 are what the count measures from.
1,290 prophetic days, solar years.
AD 508 plus 1,290 years equals AD 1798, the year Berthier took the pope and the time of the end
begins. Daniel 12-4. 1,335 prophetic days, solar years.
AD 508 plus 1,335 years equals AD 1843, the waiting year of the Great Second Advent Awakening,
immediately before the 2,300 evenings' morning's land in 1844, sitting 8.
Daniel 1211 counts from that pair of events. The historicist reading, the one this course
follows, is the reading that takes Daniel's symbols as one unbroken line of history,
and the starting year it uses here is 508, the civil year reconstructed above.
Sitting 8 showed what the daily is, Christ's continual priesthood, the work he does for
us in heaven. When Daniel 1211 speaks of the daily sacrifice being taken away,
it means that priesthood was pushed aside. A sacrifice and a priesthood are one thing here,
because the priest is the sacrifice. Jesus offered himself once, and he lives to plead that offering.
Hebrews 725. So, a power that takes away the daily removes him from his place as the one
mediator between God and men and puts a human priesthood there instead. Here, the question is
when it was taken away. The book of Daniel concludes with God's personal tender promise
to his aged beloved prophet. But go thou thy way till the end be, for thou shalt rest
and stand in thy lot at the end of the days. Daniel 1213. KJV. Daniel 1213 tells him to
go on, to rest, and at the end of the days to stand in his allotted place. A lot here is that
place, not a second verdict. The waking of those who sleep in the dust is the other promise,
Daniel 12. The prophecies of gold, silver, bronze, iron, roaring beasts, little horns,
and numbered days were never an academic puzzle. They were the historical highway leading to the
waking of sleeping bodies from the dust into everlasting fellowship with God. In plain words,
Christ stands up for his people, trouble follows, the book decides who is delivered,
and the dead awake. Interpretation.
Daniel 12 answers the question the whole book has been building toward. After the gold head,
the silver chest, the bronze belly, the iron legs, the divided feet, the four beasts,
and the little horn, what happens to the people of God? The chapter gives three answers,
and they belong together. A prince stands up for them.
Michael. The great prince which standeth for the children of thy people.
Daniel 12.1. A trouble comes such as never was. A book decides the outcome,
because the ones delivered are the ones found written in the book.
Then comes the fourth answer, the one the Old Testament had only hinted at.
Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake. Daniel 12.2.
Read the chapter in its own order, and it makes sense. The prince stands,
then the trouble comes, then deliverance, then the waking. History is not a circle,
and not a random walk. It is a road with an end, and the end is a resurrection, not a ruin.
The bottom line is personal. This chapter does not ask whether you can follow every number in it.
It asks whose book your name is in, and it answers the fear of death with a promise about dust.
Daniel himself is told to rest and to stand in his lot at the end of the days, Daniel 12.13,
which this course reads as his allotted place rather than a second trial.
The visions end where the believer ends, awake and standing.
Christ. Jesus Christ is the grand climax of the book of Daniel. Here is why each of Daniel's
titles points to him. He is the stone cut without hands that strikes the kingdoms and
fills the whole earth, Daniel 2. For that kingdom is the one that breaks every other and stands
forever. He is the fourth figure in the furnace, whose form was like the Son of God, Daniel 3.25.
He is the one like the Son of Man in Daniel 7, who comes to the ancient of days and is given
a kingdom that shall not be destroyed, the high priest receiving the kingdom in the heavenly court.
He is the prince of princes against whom the little horn stands up,
the prince whose sanctuary and daily service the horn attacks, Daniel 8.11.25.
He is the messiah cut off on Calvary's cross, called the prince in Daniel 9.25 and cut off after
the 69 weeks. And he is Michael, the great prince who stands up for his people at the end,
Daniel 12.1, which is the reading this sitting has shown from the angel's own words.
He holds the keys of death and the grave. Soon, his voice will awake the sleeping dust of every
believer who trusted in his name. We have come to the third checkpoint,
practical application, standing in your lot at the end of days.
The final chapter of Daniel speaks directly to our generation.
1. Ensure your name is recorded in the book of life. Deliverance during the coming time
of trouble depends entirely on whether your name is found written in the Lamb's Book of Life.
Do not delay your consecration. Consecration means setting your whole life apart for God,
holding nothing back, and it begins with surrender. Surrender your life to Jesus Christ today. Confess
your sins and receive his perfect righteousness. That righteousness is his own perfect record,
given to you as a gift, not a goodness you build.
Grace is God's free favor toward people who do not deserve it, and it comes to us through Jesus
Christ. If you have never done that, do it today. If you have wandered, come back.
2. Live with holy boldness while grace remains.
Michael has not yet stood up in the sense of Daniel 12.1. Hebrews 7.25 is his intercession in
this age, until that standing, when human probation closes. Grace is God's undeserved favor,
the forgiveness and help he gives through Jesus Christ, and the time of grace is the window
in which that favor may still be received. Use it to share the gospel, the good news about Jesus,
with family, friends, and neighbors, while there is still time for them to hear it and turn.
3. Shine as the brightness of the firmament. Daniel 12.3 promises,
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament,
and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
In a world darkened by moral chaos and confusion, be a beacon of truth,
pointing searching souls to Jesus Christ and his soon return.
4. Rest in the blessed hope of resurrection. When facing bereavement, illness, or mortality,
hold Daniel 12.2. Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.
Hold Daniel 12.13 for rest and a lot.
Thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.
Daniel's lot is his allotted place in the world to come,
the share God keeps for him, and he will take it up at the end of the days.
So, rest now and standing then are one promise, not two.
Hold both verses, the waking in Daniel 12.2 and the place in Daniel 12.13.
Jesus has conquered the grave, and the morning of eternity is about to break.
The principle to remember.
Text. Does Daniel 12.1 declare that Michael stands up,
a time of trouble follows, and those written in the book are delivered?
History. Did Daniel 11 accurately trace Persia,
Greece, Rome, the Papacy, and the 1798 time of the end?
Interpretation.
Does Michael standing up, Ahmad, follow Daniel 11's kingly grammar
as the prince who stands for his people? Christ.
Is Jesus Christ your king, whose resurrection guarantees that you will
awake from the dust and stand in your lot? Christology.
Michael standing up in glory and resurrection power.
The book of Daniel concludes not with an empire, a philosophical theory, or a cryptic code,
but with a living person standing up in royal majesty.
And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth
for the children of thy people. Daniel 12.1.
Michael, whose Hebrew name asks the glorious question,
Mikael, who is like God, is none other than our Lord Jesus Christ
in his warrior king and archangelic office.
He is the prince of princes who stood as commander of the Lord's host,
the one who disputed with Satan over Moses' body, Jude 9,
and who will descend with the voice of the archangel and the trump of God,
1 Thessalonians 4.16.
When Michael stands up, he stands for the children of Daniel's people,
and there follows a time of trouble such as never was.
Every person whose name is found written in the book is delivered.
Immediately following, Daniel 12.2 announces the hope,
and many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake,
some to everlasting life.
Christ's resurrection guarantees the physical, bodily resurrection
of all who sleep in him. Death does not have the final word.
Jesus has defeated the grave.
Live with your eyes fixed on the horizon for Michael's glorious standing up.
When moral confusion, geopolitical upheaval, and personal trials press upon you,
remember that the story of Daniel ends in victory, vindication, and resurrection glory.
Walk as wise teachers who turn many to righteousness,
shining as the brightness of the firmament and as the stars for ever and ever.
Daniel 12.3.
Christ is standing for you today in heaven, and soon he will stand to take you home.
